become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not clearly linked to the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery, and no other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal item provides a plausible religious cue or meaning that would explain this highly specific avoidance.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat profile centers on generalized hypervigilance after robbery, but specifically listening for someone entering the home implies a home-intrusion context that is unsupported by the trauma type and by the rest of the selected items; this makes the item hard to reconcile with the same indexed event.

vignette: Jamil had always felt a sense of purpose in their work as a veterinarian. There was something about helping animals heal that brought them a sense of calm and fulfillment. But all of that changed one evening when they were walking home from the clinic. A group of strangers approached Jamil, their faces obscured by hoods, and demanded their wallet and phone. Jamil tried to comply, but in the chaos, one of the assailants knocked them to the ground, leaving them with a throbbing head and a shattered sense of safety. In the aftermath, Jamil found themselves struggling to shake off the feeling of vulnerability that lingered long after the physical wounds had healed. They began to notice that they were constantly scanning their surroundings for signs of danger - checking alleys, watching strangers' hands, flinching at sudden noises. Even in the comfort of their own home, Jamil felt on edge, as if an attack could come at any moment. "What if someone is hiding behind the couch?" they would catch themselves thinking. Jamil tried to reason with themselves that the chances of such a thing happening again were slim, but their mind wouldn't be swayed. They started to avoid going out unless absolutely necessary, relying on their partner to run errands and socialize. "It's just not worth it," Jamil would say, when asked why they didn't want to join friends for dinner or meet up at a park. As the weeks turned into months, Jamil noticed that even small things could trigger memories of the mugging. A whiff of cigarette smoke might transport them back to that night, and they'd feel their heart racing all over again. Trying to recount what had happened became increasingly difficult - they would lose track of the details mid-sentence, as if the memory itself was too painful to confront head-on. Jamil found themselves oscillating between denial ("It wasn't that bad," they'd tell themselves) and hypervigilance (checking over their shoulder for potential threats). When feeling threatened or anxious, Jamil had a tendency to become overly compliant - agreeing to do favors for others even when it didn't feel right. This coping mechanism only left them feeling drained and resentful. As time went on, the strain of these behaviors began to show in other areas of Jamil's life. Their relationship with their partner started to fray as they withdrew further into themselves. Colleagues at the clinic noticed a change in Jamil's demeanor - once warm and confident, now distant and guarded. The constant fear that "something bad could happen next" made it hard for Jamil to focus on anything else. One day, while tending to an injured cat, Jamil realized they couldn't shake off the sense of despair that had settled over them since the mugging. They used to be a happy person - someone who loved nothing more than fixing broken animals and watching them thrive. But now? "I just feel lost," Jamil confided in their partner. That was when they decided it was time to seek help, not knowing where else to turn or how to quiet the constant voice in their head warning of impending danger. For Jamil, seeking therapy wasn't about being "cured" but about finding a way back to themselves - to rediscover that sense of purpose and joy they once had. They hoped it wouldn't be too late to reclaim their life from the shadows of that fateful night.
